audio_caption: The clip begins with a female speaker who sounds enthusiastic stating that the "funnest part of your CBC is making blood smears," although that is often considered a challenge. She assures the audience that any issues will be resolved by the end of the video. She emphasizes the need for a well-mixed, unclotted EDTA tube, and recommends gently mixing it rather than shaking. She suggests checking for clots with an applicator stick, explaining that it can determine if the sample is good.

The clip begins with a female speaker highlighting the importance of "beveled slides" for making good blood smears and emphasizing that they can be used even when economy is a concern. The speaker continues by addressing how to get a "well-filled PCV tube" with a "decent size drop" and discusses the issues with both too small and too large drops, emphasizing the importance of getting the "blood drop just right." She advises on how to fill the tube properly, then describes the ideal placement of a medium-sized drop on a frosted edge slide.

A woman is lecturing on blood smears, stating she's "going to show some of the 'don'ts'" and explaining "pitfalls" in slide preparation. She describes a common error called the "Olympic ski jump technique," mentioning how people leave the slide by the head, ending up with "line preparation," which isn't good for blood smears. She continues giving examples of bad blood smearing techniques, such as admiring your work slowly, suggesting that going faster is better. She advocates for using both sides and ends of slides. The woman goes on to describe more common mistakes like going right off the edge of the slide and then using the "race car rev," describing that one is a waste of time and might make people anxious. The speaker ends the lecture by commenting on how to save energy.

A woman speaks in a calm, informative tone, explaining that "people will pull instead of push to make their smears," which results in uneven shapes and less control. She emphasizes that this method is not recommended, noting the thick smear produced. She then cautions against applying too much pressure, warning about a grinding sound. The woman describes "my shaky slide syndrome," explaining that holding the spreader too high reduces control and causes wobbling. She says she will show the right way to do it and the clip ends by stating "everything will be forever lovely".

There is a female speaker. She talks about having "3 Goldilocks properly sized drops." She then explains the best way to smear blood on a slide. She advises the listener to "anchor your side with your index finger" and to "push it out as fast as you can." She then gives an analogy: "Usain Bolt in a 100 meter dash." She then reiterates the technique, saying, "Jam the spreader into the end of the slide and your index finger," and then says that this should result in good slide preparation after that with your thumb nail shape.

The clip starts with a female speaker discussing submitting a poor slide is better than no slide at all because cells disintegrate overnight. She suggests keeping blood smears separate from any formalin-containing vessels as it "wrecks the cells". She mentions slide containers that can be mailed and advises to protect them from "flies, dirt, water", and slides from each other. The speaker then stresses the importance of labeling samples.

The audio begins with a female speaker, discussing the importance of including animal identification on samples, such as the owner and patient names, emphasizing it's preferable due to common names like "Daisy". She also mentions that adding the date to the tube or requisition is necessary because there is a time limit for processing samples. Next, the speaker continues, stating that once smears are air-dried, they can be stained. She clarifies that if sending samples to a reference lab, it's best to leave them unstained.

The audio clip begins with a female speaker giving instructions. The instructions involve dipping items into a set of solutions five times, with one second per dip. She mentions that the final solution is water and emphasizes cleanliness at the end.

The audio clip features a female speaker advising on stain order, emphasizing starting "from lightest to darkest." She then describes dipping something "very slowly and patiently." Background sounds suggest the tinkling of metal, which may be related to the dipping process. The speech is instructional and calm.
A female speaker describes a process that involves a "combination of dipping and swirling." She advises to "let it air dry," followed by blotting the bottom and wiping the back.

The clip starts with a calm, informative female voice discussing the process of protecting slides in a lab, mentioning the use of mounting media and coverslips after staining. This is followed by the distinct sound of something being peeled, suggesting a protective film being removed from an object. Finally, the clip ends with what sounds like a cat meowing, adding an unexpected element to the scene and potentially indicating the presence of a cat in the background.
